about: Engineering Challenges is the first module of UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme: a 15-credit, Term 1 module (2026/27 module catalogue) built around two design projects, the first based in your own department and the second interdisciplinary; UCL's IEP pages describe them as two five-week projects. It has no lecture syllabus to revise; it develops research, feedback, presentation, teamwork, project management and an awareness of social impact through project work. In 2026/27 it is assessed by coursework (40%, two assessments), group activity (50%, three assessments) and another form of assessment (10%). This guide explains the module and gives general design and project tools to help you prepare; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What Engineering Challenges is and how it is assessed
notes.body:
Engineering Challenges (ENGF0001) is the opening module of UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme (IEP), the shared first-year framework for students in Biochemical, Biomedical, Chemical, Civil, Electronic and Electrical, and Mechanical Engineering and in Computer Science. It is a 15-credit, Term 1 module at FHEQ Level 4, taught in person, and in 2026/27 it is open only to IEP students.

How it is structured
- It is problem-based: you learn by working on open-ended design problems rather than from a lecture syllabus. UCL describes it as the first problem-based learning activity you meet, starting on the first day of classes.
- It is built around two five-week design projects. UCL's undergraduate pages say you spend about four hours a week in class on the Challenge, alongside your other lectures, and that themes are drawn from UCL Grand Challenges topics such as sustainability and global health.
- Challenge 1 runs in the first five weeks and is based in your own department, on a topic linked to research done there. It introduces information gathering, giving and receiving feedback, and presenting your work. Note that the 2026/27 catalogue calls it a department-based "individual" project, while UCL's "How we teach" page describes both Challenges as team projects (with Challenge 1 teammates from your own programme cohort), so check your Challenge 1 brief to see exactly which parts are marked individually.
- Challenge 2 is interdisciplinary. Departments are paired or grouped to work on different aspects of one large project, and you consider the social impact of your solution as well as making sure it works technically. It introduces teamwork, communication and basic project management.
- The module is taught alongside Design and Professional Skills I and Mathematical Modelling and Analysis I, and material is cross-referenced between all three, so skills from those modules (for example technical drawing or modelling) are expected to show up in your Challenge work.

Assessment (2026/27 catalogue)
- 40% coursework (two assessments).
- 50% group activity (three assessments).
- 10% other form of assessment (the catalogue does not say what).
- Marks are numeric. The catalogue does not say what each individual assessment is, so read each brief on Moodle carefully for deliverables, word limits, deadlines and marking criteria.

What it is trying to develop
The stated outcomes include understanding your discipline and its place in the world, understanding the design process and the relationship between engineering and society, gathering information and applying design, communicating effectively, solving problems creatively and critically, and working in teams, including interdisciplinary ones.

How to approach it
- Treat the marking criteria as your specification. Before starting, list what each deliverable must contain and who marks it.
- Keep a dated log of research, decisions and meetings from week one. It makes reports, reflections and peer assessment much easier.
- Expect ambiguity. Part of the point is learning to define the problem yourself, state your assumptions and justify choices with evidence.

Exam tips: there is no exam listed for this module in 2026/27; the marks come from coursework and group work, so steady effort across the five-week blocks matters more than a final push.

notes.h: Challenge 1: researching, giving feedback and presenting
notes.body:
Challenge 1 introduces three skills you will use for the rest of the degree: gathering information, giving and receiving feedback, and presenting.

Researching and gathering information
- Start by restating the problem in your own words: who has the problem, what a good outcome looks like, and what the constraints are (cost, safety, materials, regulation, time).
- Separate primary sources (data you collect: measurements, surveys, interviews, tests) from secondary sources (published work: journal papers, standards, reports, textbooks, manufacturers' data).
- Use UCL Library Services search and databases rather than relying only on general web searches; check who wrote a source, when, and what evidence it gives.
- Record full references as you go. Use one consistent referencing style (follow your department's guidance) and never present others' words or figures as your own.
- Turn research into requirements: each finding should change something in your design specification or justify a decision.

Giving and receiving feedback
- Good feedback is specific (points at a particular slide, calculation or sentence), evidence-based, and suggests a next step.
- When receiving feedback, listen first, ask clarifying questions, and record what you will change and why. You do not have to accept every comment, but you should be able to justify ignoring one.
- Peer review sessions are a chance to see how others interpreted the same brief; use them to test whether your argument is clear to someone who has not lived with it.

Presenting work
- Structure: problem, what you found, what you propose, why it works, what the limitations are, what comes next.
- One message per slide, with readable figures (labelled axes, units, sources) and minimal text.
- Rehearse to time. Know your numbers well enough to answer questions on assumptions and uncertainty.
- If presenting as a group, plan the hand-overs and make sure everyone can answer questions on the whole design, not only their part.

How to prepare before term
- Look at your department's research themes on its website; Challenge 1 topics are linked to them.
- Practise summarising a short technical article in five sentences, and making a simple chart in a spreadsheet or in code.
- Get comfortable with the library catalogue and a reference manager if you want one.

Exam tips: in written deliverables, examiners reward a clear line from evidence to decision. Every claim should be backed by a reference, a calculation or a test result.

notes.h: Challenge 2: interdisciplinary teamwork and social impact
notes.body:
In Challenge 2, departments are paired or grouped to work on different parts of a single large project. You work with students from other engineering disciplines and must consider the social impact of your solution, not only whether it works technically. The module also introduces basic project management tools and practices.

Working in an interdisciplinary team
- Different disciplines use different vocabularies and priorities. Agree early on a shared problem statement, a glossary of key terms and a single set of units.
- Make interfaces explicit. When your sub-system depends on another group's output (a load, a voltage, a flow rate, a data format), write that interface down with values and tolerances, and agree who owns it.
- Hold short, regular meetings with an agenda, decisions and named actions; keep minutes in a shared folder.
- Split roles clearly (for example coordinator, technical leads, document editor) but rotate or share tasks so everyone understands the whole design.
- Expect conflict about priorities. Resolve it with agreed criteria (see the decision matrix in the next note) rather than by who argues loudest.

A widely taught model of team development is Bruce Tuckman's (1965): forming, storming, norming and performing, with adjourning added in 1977. It is a description, not a rule, but it helps to recognise that early friction is normal.

Thinking about social impact
- Identify stakeholders: users, people affected but not paying, operators, maintainers, regulators, communities, and the environment.
- Consider the whole life cycle: materials and manufacture, use, maintenance, and end of life.
- Ask who benefits and who bears the costs or risks; whether the solution is accessible and affordable to its intended users; and what could go wrong if it is misused or fails.
- Use evidence for impact claims (data, published studies, consultation) rather than general statements.

Showing technical credibility
- Back the concept with calculations, simple models or prototype tests, and state assumptions.
- Prototypes do not need to be polished: a quick model that tests one risky assumption is often more valuable than a pretty one.

Group assessment
Group activity carries 50% of the module mark in 2026/27. Keep evidence of your own contribution (commits, drafts, minutes, logbook) in case peer assessment or individual reflection forms part of the brief.

Exam tips: in a group report, write a short section showing how each discipline's work fits together, with the interface values. Markers look for an integrated design, not several separate reports stapled together.

notes.h: Design tools: specifications, decision matrices and project planning
notes.body:
Engineering Challenges draws on experimental methods, modelling and prototyping. Whatever the brief, a few standard design and project management tools will help you structure the work and justify decisions. These are general engineering tools, not a module syllabus.

The design process
Most models share the same loop: understand the need, define requirements, generate concepts, evaluate and select, develop and test, then communicate and iterate. Real projects go round the loop several times; testing usually sends you back to revise requirements or concepts.

Product design specification (PDS)
- A list of requirements the design must meet, written so they can be checked: "must support 50 kg with no permanent deformation" rather than "must be strong".
- Distinguish demands (must) from wishes (desirable), and give a source or reason for each.

Generating and selecting concepts
- Generate several genuinely different concepts before choosing (sketching, brainstorming, morphological charts).
- A weighted decision matrix scores each concept against criteria from the PDS. Each score is multiplied by the criterion's weight, and the products are added. Weights should be agreed before scoring, to avoid bias.
- Example: weights cost 0.5, performance 0.3, safety 0.2. Concept A scores 9, 6, 6 → 4.5 + 1.8 + 1.2 = 7.5. Concept B scores 6, 8, 9 → 3.0 + 2.4 + 1.8 = 7.2. A wins, even though B has the larger unweighted total (23 against 21).
- Do a quick sensitivity check: if a small change in weights reverses the ranking, say so.

Planning the work
- Break the work into tasks with durations and dependencies (a work breakdown structure).
- A Gantt chart shows tasks as bars against time, with milestones such as deadlines.
- The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks; it sets the shortest possible project duration. Tasks on it have no float (slack), so any delay to them delays the project.
- Example: A (3 days) must finish before B (2 days) and C (4 days); D (1 day) needs both B and C. Path A–C–D takes 8 days and A–B–D takes 6, so the critical path is A–C–D at 8 days, and B has 2 days of float.
- Use SMART objectives (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) for team tasks.

Prototyping and testing
- Decide what question each prototype answers. Record the test method, results and what you changed as a result.

Exam tips: show your working for any matrix or schedule in the report, including weights, scores and the dependency list, so markers can follow your reasoning.

questions.q: Task A (3 days) must be finished before tasks B (2 days) and C (4 days) can start. Task D (1 day) can start only when both B and C are finished. What is the minimum project duration?
questions.why: The two paths are A–B–D (3 + 2 + 1 = 6 days) and A–C–D (3 + 4 + 1 = 8 days). The project cannot finish before its longest path, so 8 days is the minimum and A–C–D is the critical path. 10 days adds every task as if they all ran one after another, ignoring that B and C can run in parallel. 6 days is the shorter path A–B–D, which would leave C unfinished. 7 days is A followed by C, forgetting task D at the end.

questions.q: Criteria weights are cost 0.5, performance 0.3 and safety 0.2. Concept A scores 9, 6, 6; concept B scores 6, 8, 9 (same order). Which concept wins, with what score?
questions.why: Weighted totals: A = 0.5 × 9 + 0.3 × 6 + 0.2 × 6 = 7.5; B = 0.5 × 6 + 0.3 × 8 + 0.2 × 9 = 7.2, so A wins with 7.5. Concept B with 23 adds the raw scores and ignores the weights. Concept B with 8.1 applies the weights in reverse order (0.2 to cost and 0.5 to safety). Concept A with 4.5 counts only the most heavily weighted criterion, cost, and leaves out the other two.
